headline: Recommended City Council amend Chapter 28 marijuana retail rules on equity standards; shopping cart ordinance continued to November 2, 2026.
summary: Members recommended a 2-0 amendment to Chapter 28 on marijuana retail establishments, with equity standards and a municipal equity plan. They continued the shopping cart ordinance to November 2, 2026, after discussing locks on carts and possible fines. They also recommended Angela Sanfilippo for the Fisheries Commission.
decisions: Recommended the City Council appoint Angela Sanfilippo to the Fisheries Commission, TTE 2/15/2029, by a 2-0 vote with one absent.
Continued the shopping cart ordinance proposal, CC#2026-017, to November 2, 2026.
Recommended the City Council amend Chapter 28 Marijuana Retail Establishments by adding Article II on equity standards, by a 2-0 vote with one absent.

Present: Chair, Councilor Sean Nolan; Vice Chair; Councilor Tony Gross
Absent: Councilor Frank Margiotta; Councilor Marjorie Grace
Other Councilors Present: Councilor Dylan Benson
Also Present: General Counsel, Suzanne Egan

2. CC#2026-017 (Benson): Amend GCO Ch. 14 “Offenses and Miscellaneous Provisions” by
ADDING a new Article IV “Shopping Cart Regulations,” Sec. 14-46 “Definitions,” Sec. 14-47
“Identification of shopping carts,” Sec. 14-48 “Shopping carts to be confined to premises,” Sec.
14-49 “Enforcement.” (cont. from September 14, 2026)
Summary of Discussion: Councilor Benson stated that after the last meeting regarding the matter, he had
reached out to stores that would be affected by the proposed ordinance change. He stated that there wasn’t
pushback, but managers had to reach out to their corporate offices. He stated that constituents had reached
out with pictures of shopping carts that had been abandoned around the City. He stated that he had updated
the proposed ordinance amendment to require a locking system on carts, rather than penalize businesses who
have their carts stolen and taken off site. He stated that businesses would have six months to comply with the
proposed ordinance. 
Councilor Gross stated that businesses could choose to simply pay the fine rather than retrofit their carts.
Councilor Benson stated that there had not been any pushback from the businesses that he had spoken with.
Councilor Gross asked if Stop & Shop had given an opinion on the matter. Councilor Benson stated that
they had not and said they needed to speak with the corporate offices. He stated that stores in other
O&A Committee October 19, 2026 Page 2 of 6
communities had locks on their carts so it would not be hard for stores to adapt. He stated that he had found
twenty other nearby communities with similar ordinances requiring locks. 
Councilor Nolan stated that he did not currently support the proposed amendment. He stated that he wanted
to see the response from the corporate offices before moving forward with the matter. He stated that a penalty
for those who stole carts and walked around the City with them could be added. He stated that with the
increased cost of groceries, stores may further raise prices to offset the cost of retrofitting carts, which would
put a burden on residents. He asked that more information be provided on communication with stores that
would be affected.
Councilor Gross stated that penalizing stores for their stolen property did not help the City’s attempts at
brining more grocery stores to the City. Councilor Benson stated that the proposed ordinance had been
updated and only required locks on carts, and there would only be a fine if carts did not have locks on them,
not if the carts were stolen.
Councilor Gross stated that an individual could steal a cart and smash the lock. Councilor Benson stated
that he had spoken with the City of Somerville who has had a similar ordinance for ten years, and they had
no issues like that occur. 
Councilor Gross suggested that smaller carts not be required to have a lock, as smaller carts may be less
desirable to steal, and it would put less of a burden on smaller stores. He stated that another limiting factor
could be the number of carts a business has, such as 50 or less a store wouldn’t be required to install locks. 
Councilor Nolan stated that more work should be done on the ordinance amendment before a vote was taken.
He stated that a cart minimum for the ordinance, as well as a penalty for those who were in possession of
stolen carts should be added.
There was a brief discussion regarding enforcement of the proposed ordinance.
This matter was continued to the November 2, 2026 Ordinance & Administration meeting.
3. Memorandum from General Counsel proposing an amendment to Chapter 28 Marijuana Retail
Establishments
Summary of Discussion: General Counsel, Suzanne Egan stated that the proposed ordinance amendment
was a mandate from the State. She stated that the purpose of the ordinance was to allow for transparency in
the permitting and licensing process. She stated that the ordinance was also meant to rectify the negative
impact that the criminalization of marijuana had. She stated that this would outline within the ordinance the
permitting process for marijuana establishments. She stated that the ordinance would also outline how a social
equity application would be permitted. 
Councilor Gross stated that he had been unable to find a definition for a verified social equity business.
Suzanne Egan stated that the State defined several groups that were disadvantaged, such as ones owned by
minorities, women, and veterans. 
Councilor Gross asked if there was an equity plan in place. Suzanne Egan stated that the Cannabis Control
Commission had a model equity plan that the City would adopt.

COMMITTEE RECOMMENDATION:  On a motion by Councilor Nolan, seconded by Councilor Gross, 
the Ordinances & Administration Committee voted 2 in favor, 0 opposed, 1 absent, to recommend that the 
City Council amend the Gloucester Code of Ordinances Chapter 28 “MARIJUANA RETAIL 
ESTABLISHMENTS” as follows:
Chapter 28 MARIJUANA RETAIL ESTABLISHMENTS
ADD ARTICLE II. – EQUITY STANDARDS FOR PROMOTING AND ENCOURAGING FULL 
PARTICIPATION IN THE REGULATED MARIJUANA INDUSTRY
Sec. 28-3. Legislative Authority
This ordinance is authorized pursuant to St. 2022, c. 180, an act relative to equity in the cannabis industry, 
M.G.L. c. 94G and M.G.L. c. 94I, 935 CMR §§ 500.000, and §§ 501.000. 
Sec. 28-4. Purpose
The intent of this ordinance is to comply with M.G.L. c. 94G § 4(a) and 935 CMR 500.181 and 501.181.
Sec. 28-5. Applicability
This ordinance shall apply to all individuals and entities seeking to locate a marijuana establishment or 
medical marijuana treatment center within the City. No individual or entity shall operate a marijuana 
establishment or a medical marijuana treatment center unless duly licensed to do so by the Cannabis 
Control Commission. Nothing in this section shall be construed to supersede federal and state laws 
governing the sale and distribution of marijuana.
Sec. 28-6. Definitions
The definitions set forth in M.G.L. c. 94I § 1, M.G.L. c. 94G § 1, 935 CMR §§ 500.002, §§ 501.002, §§ 
500.181(4)(a), and §§ 501.181(4)(a) are incorporated herein by reference.  
Sec. 28-7. Transparency of Local Approval Process:
(1) Data shall be published regarding the number and composition of applicants, identifying each pre-
verified or verified social equity business, social equity program participant, or economic 
empowerment priority applicant.
(2) The following information shall be published in a conspicuous location at City offices and on the 
City website:
(a) All required steps of the local approval process including, but not limited to, all associated 
fees, deadlines, and meeting schedules for local bodies involved in the local approval 
process;
(b) Identification of key individuals involved in the local approval process, including, but not 
limited to, their name, title, business address, and business contact information such as 
email address or phone number; 
(c) A list of all documentation required by the local approval process, in downloadable form 
and paper form; 
(d) Identification of application criteria for local approval to operate a marijuana establishment 
or medical marijuana treatment center, and scoring methodologies relied on by the City;
O&A Committee October 19, 2026 Page 4 of 6
(e) General and individual scoring information for all license applicants;
(f) An explanation, in narrative form, of its reasoning for the approval or denial of an 
application; and
(g) Any other information required by the Commission as outlined in 935 CMR §§ 500.000 
and §§ 501.000.
Sec. 28-8. Practices for Host Community Agreement Negotiations
Host community agreement negotiations with individuals or entities pre-verified or verified as social equity 
businesses, and license applicants that have been designated as social equity program participants or 
economic empowerment priority applicants shall include but not be limited to, the following: 
(1) A standard evaluation form, or use a form developed by the Cannabis Control Commission, that 
scores components of an application. The evaluation form shall include consideration of equity in 
the overall evaluation score which must comprise not less than 25% of the total evaluation score. 
(2) This equity component shall include:
a. whether an individual, entity, or license applicant is pre-verified or verified by the 
Cannabis Control Commission as a social equity business; 
b. whether the license applicant is a social equity program participant;
c. whether the license applicant is an economic empowerment priority applicant;
d. whether a license applicant or pre-verified individual or entity has a prior marijuana-related
criminal offense or conviction;
e. whether a license applicant or pre-verified individual or entity is part of an area of 
disproportionate Impact, as identified by the Cannabis Control Commission; or whether a 
pre-verified individual is of Black, African American, Hispanic, Latino, Native American 
or indigenous descent, or a majority of a pre-verified entity or license applicant entity is 
comprised of individuals that are of Black, African American, Hispanic, Latino, Native 
American or indigenous descent.
(3) If additional marijuana establishments or medical marijuana treatment centers are allowed, at least 
50% of those licenses, but no less than one license, above the previously established cap shall be 
reserved for license applicants that are pre-verified or verified social equity businesses, social 
equity program participants, economic empowerment priority applicants, or all.
Sec. 28-9. Equity Standards for Host Community Agreements
(1) Negotiations of host community agreements with equity parties shall be prioritized. For the 
purposes of negotiations of a host community agreement for an application for licensure, equity 
parties are as follows:
a. A license applicant that is pre-verified or verified as a social equity business; or
b. A license applicant that has been designated as social equity program participants, 
economic empowerment priority applicants, or both. 
(2) Fees may be waived or reduced for an equity party to a host community agreement negotiation, 
including, but not limited to community impact fees, zoning, and occupancy fees.
(3) During host community agreement negotiations with an equity party the following shall occur:
a. Engage in an ongoing dialogue by providing multiple opportunities for discussion and 
negotiation of host community agreement terms including, at minimum, two conferences 
with an equity party;
O&A Committee October 19, 2026 Page 5 of 6
b. Include any attorney, authorized representative, or other advocate, if elected by an equity 
party, in all negotiation discussions and conferences; 
c. Promote language access by providing a certified interpreter or translator to assist an equity
party who is a non-English speaker during all negotiation discussions and conferences;
d. Provide reasonable opportunities for an equity party to review a proposed host community 
agreement, term, or condition, outside of a negotiation conference, or to seek review or 
input by a third party of their choice;
e. Negotiate the terms of a host community agreement in good faith, including consideration 
of flexible terms that may mitigate particular challenges affecting an equity party, such as 
access to capital, with all terms and clauses conspicuously identified and openly discussed; 
and  
f. Allow an equity party to propose an amendment to, or seek cancellation of, a host 
community agreement within thirty days from the date of execution of the host community 
agreement. 
(4) The negotiations may also:
a. Expedite or prioritize the local approval process for social equity businesses, social equity 
program participants, and economic empowerment priority applicants;  
b. Provide technical assistance for social equity businesses, social equity program 
participants, and economic empowerment priority applicants navigating the local approval 
process;  
c. Designate a municipal contact who shall work closely with social equity businesses, social 
equity program participants, and economic empowerment priority applicants in the local 
approval process from initial inquiry through the end of the permitting process; or  
d. Adopt an exclusivity period to permit social equity businesses for three years or until the 
goals of the exclusivity period have been met as determined by the municipality. 
(5) Negotiations shall not:
a. Use or employ undue influence, duress, coercion, intimidation, threats, or any strong-arm 
tactics;
b. Threaten loss of an equity party's position in its local application queue or delay to the 
processing of an equity party's application;
c. Compel an equity party to sign a host community agreement in any manner that conflicts 
with the practices required through applicable state law and regulations; and 
d. Negotiate or discontinue negotiations with an equity party in bad faith.
Sec. 28-10. Municipal Equity Plan
(1) An equity plan shall be developed to promote and encourage full participation in the regulated 
cannabis industry by individuals from communities disproportionately harmed by cannabis 
prohibition and enforcement. 
(2) The equity plan shall be publicized at City Hall and on the City’s website.
(3) The equity plan shall
a. Encourage applications from business and individuals that would meet the definition of 
social equity businesses, social equity program participants, and Economic empowerment 
priority applicants as determined by the Commission; and
O&A Committee October 19, 2026 Page 6 of 6
b. Include goals, programs, and measurements the City will utilize to promote and encourage 
equity participation.
Sec. 28-11. Notification
Notification of this this ordinance and any other information shall be provided to the Cannabis Control 
Commission as required by applicable state law and regulations in a timely manner.
Sec. 28-12. Implementation
This ordinance shall not be implemented in a manner that conflicts or interferes with the M.G.L. c. 94G or 
c. 94I, or with the regulations promulgated thereunder, including 935 CMR §§ 500.000 or §§ 501.000.
Sec. 28-13. Severability
If any provisions of this ordinance shall be held to be invalid, those provisions shall be severable, and the 
remaining sections shall be valid with full force and effect.
A public hearing for this matter will be held November 10, 2026
